p: Abu Tahir Sulayman was an Arabized Persian, born in June or July 906 at Ganaveh on the coast of Fars. His father, Abu Sa'id, a tribal leader taught by Hamdan Qarmat of Kufa, had begun the militarization of the Qarmatians.

Most Arabic sources agree that Abu Sa'id named his eldest son, Abu'l-Qasim Sa'id, as heir and that Abu Tahir revolted against him and usurped power. Another tradition, reported by the Kufan anti-Isma'ili polemicist Ibn Rizam, holds that Sa'id was only a regent and handed over power in 917/918, when his brother was barely ten. It is likely that power was nominally shared among all the sons, with Abu Tahir dominant. Abu'l-Qasim was not executed and lived until 972.

In 926 he led his army as far north as Kufa and made the Abbasids pay large sums for him to leave. On his return he built palaces at Ahsa and declared it his permanent capital. In 928 Caliph al-Muqtadir sent against him the generals Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj, Mu'nis al-Muzaffar and Harun, who were beaten and driven back to Baghdad.

At Mecca in 930 he was at first refused entry, invoked the right of all Muslims to enter and swore that he came in peace. Once inside, his men rode into the Masjid al-Haram, massacred the pilgrims, set fire to the Kaaba and threw bodies into the Zamzam Well. The attack was believed to be meant to prompt the appearance of the Mahdi and followed millenarian excitement over the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter in 928.

The Mahdi he recognised in 931, Abu'l-Fadl al-Isfahani, a prisoner who claimed descent from the Sasanian kings, restored the veneration of fire, burned religious books and had members of Bahrayn's notable families executed. In one account Abu Tahir's mother exposed him and his brother Sa'id killed him after eighty days; in others Abu Tahir denounced him as a false Mahdi and had him executed.

Abu Tahir took back control of the state and resumed his attacks on pilgrims crossing Arabia. He rejected the attempts of both the Abbasids and the Fatimids to persuade him to return the Black Stone. He died of smallpox in 944, aged about 38, and was succeeded by his three surviving sons and his nephews. According to the historian al-Juwayni the stone came back in 951, thrown in a sack into the Great Mosque of Kufa with a note: "By command we took it, and by command we have brought it back." Its removal had broken it into seven pieces.

notes: The article dates the Kufa campaign 927 in its lede and 926 in the body; I used the body's 926.

Return of the Black Stone: the article says the Abbasids ransomed it in 952 and, in the next sentence, that al-Juwayni has it returned in 951; I gave al-Juwayni's 951, attributed, as the existing entry has 951.
The polemicist's full name in the article is Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Rizam al-Ta'i; shortened to Ibn Rizam.
No number of dead at Mecca is given in the article (the 20,000 is for the 906 caravan ambush, before his rule); none given here.
The Basra attacks (lede: 923; body undated: grand mosque destroyed, marketplace burned) are left out for length, as the existing entry already names the Basra raid.
